opus-5.5.text:
I think they're complementary, and it helps to put them on two different axes. Neural architecture search looks at the structure of the network: how many layers, what kinds of operations, how they connect. Our work on model zoos and hyper-representations holds the architecture fixed and asks a different question. Given a population of trained networks, what can we learn about the space of weights itself?

In NAS you usually still have to train each candidate architecture from scratch, or at least partially, to know whether it's good. That's where most of the compute goes. We've been looking at it the other way around. If we train representation learners, essentially autoencoders, on thousands of trained models, we learn a latent space in which the weights live. From that space we can predict properties like accuracy or generalization gap without running data through the model. And more interestingly, we can sample new weights that perform well, or that are good initializations, so training converges faster than with a random init.

So in a sense, NAS searches over the "skeleton" and we search over the "muscle." Long term I think the two should merge. Imagine a system that proposes an architecture and also directly generates weights for it, or at least a very good starting point. Then the expensive inner loop of NAS, training every candidate, could largely be replaced by generation.

There are open challenges, of course. Today our methods work best within one architecture family, because the weight space has to be somewhat aligned. Permutation symmetries in neurons make that hard, so we have to deal with them through augmentation or alignment. Generalizing across architectures, so that a single model understands weights from different shapes of networks, is exactly where it starts to touch NAS. That's one of the directions we're most excited about: treating neural networks themselves as a data modality, with model zoos as datasets, and learning from that population the way we learn from images or text.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says weight generation and neural architecture search are complementary, then distinguishes their roles: NAS searches network structure while weight generation learns and samples from the space of weights.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's one we get a lot, because on the surface they look like they're in the same neighborhood. But I'd actually say they're attacking almost orthogonal problems.

Neural architecture search is about the structure. You're asking, what should the graph of the network look like? How many layers, what kind of operations, how wide, where do the skip connections go? And once you've found that structure, you still have to train it from scratch. The search is over architectures, and the weights are just a byproduct of whatever training run you do afterwards.

What we're doing with weight generation, with our work on hyper-representations, is kind of the inverse. We hold the architecture fixed and we ask, what does the space of trained weights look like for this architecture? Because if you train the same network a thousand times with different seeds, different data, different hyperparameters, you get a thousand points in this very high-dimensional weight space. And it turns out that space has structure. It's not just noise. So we learn a representation of that space, an embedding essentially, and then we can sample from it. We can generate new weights that, when you drop them into the network, already perform reasonably well before you've done any gradient steps.

So one way I like to frame it is, NAS is searching for the right container, and we're learning what to put in the container. And I think the exciting part is that these are complementary. You could imagine a world where you do architecture search and then, instead of paying the full cost of training every candidate from scratch, you generate a good initialization from a learned prior over weights. That would make the search itself a lot cheaper, because evaluating a candidate architecture is exactly the expensive part of NAS.

The other thing I'd say is that there's a conceptual shift here. NAS still treats training as the thing that produces the model. We're starting to treat trained weights themselves as a data modality, something you can learn from, generate, and manipulate directly. And once you make that shift, a lot of other things open up, like predicting a model's properties just from its weights, or transferring knowledge between models without going through the data at all.

astra-6.text:
I see them as complementary. Neural architecture search asks, “What should the structure of the network look like?” Our work asks, “Can we generate the weights for a network, rather than learn them from scratch every time?” So we’re looking at a different part of the problem.

One of the expensive steps in architecture search is training candidate networks to find out how well they perform. If you could generate useful initial weights, you could potentially reduce that cost. But generating weights across different architectures is itself a challenge: the dimensions change, the connectivity changes, and you need a representation that can handle that.

So I wouldn’t say weight generation replaces architecture search. The interesting possibility is to bring the two together—to search for a structure while also using what we’ve learned from previously trained networks to give it a useful starting point.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as complementary. Neural architecture search asks, what is the right structure for a network? Our work asks, given a structure, can we generate weights that already give you a useful starting point, instead of initializing randomly and training from scratch?

The idea is to learn from a population of trained networks—to capture something about the solutions they have found in weight space, and then use that representation to generate new weights. Of course, architecture matters, because it determines the shape and organization of those weights. So generating weights across different architectures is a more challenging problem.

Where the two could come together is in the search process itself. If you could generate useful weights for a candidate architecture, you might reduce the amount of training needed to evaluate it. So architecture search explores the structure, and weight generation could help make that exploration more efficient.
